Abstract
26
Pterostilbene as a functional food ingredient is limited by low water-solubility and 
27
low bioaccessibility. Recently, there is a growing interest to use nanoemulsions to 
28
encapsulate hydrophobic compounds. In particular, lipid type plays a critical role in 
29
the efficacy of nanoemulsions. In this study, three different lipids (medium chain 
30
triglycerides (MCT), sunflower oil, and olive oil) were each used as carrier lipids to 
31
fabricate nanoemulsions for delivery of pterostilbene. The impact of carrier lipid 
32
composition on the physical stability, in vitro digestion of each pterostilbene-loaded 
33
nanoemulsions was studied. Their effect on pterostilbene bioaccessibility and Caco-2 
34
cell monolayer permeability of pterostilbene was also investigated. The saturation 
35
concentrations of pterostilbene in three lipids were firstly determined. Nanoemulsions 
36
were subjected to in vitro digestion using a model simulating the gastrointestinal tract. 
37
Mixed micelles thus were obtained and analyzed for intestinal epithelial permeability 
38
using Caco-2 cell monolayer model. The saturation solubility of pterostilbene in the 
39
tested lipids was ranked as follows: MCT > sunflower oil ≈ olive oil. The extent of 
40
free fatty acids release during lipid digestion decreased as follows: MCT > sunflower 
41
oil > olive oil. Bioaccessibility of pterostilbene followed a similar trend. The highest 
42
apparent permeability coefficient of pterostilbene was observed in MCT micelles, 
43
followed by sunflower oil or olive oil micelles. Our study indicated that 
44
nanoemulsions fabricated with MCT were more effective for delivering pterostilbene 
45
than those produced with long chain triglycerides. Moreover, for long chain 
46
triglycerides, the higher unsaturation levels of lipid improved the lipid digestibility 
47
and pterostilbene bioaccessibility.

1. Introduction
51
Pterostilbene (trans-3,5-dimethoxy-4’-hydroxystilbene, Fig. 1A), a dimethylated 
52
analog of resveratrol (trans-3,5,4’-trihydroxystilbene, Fig. 1B), is a naturally 
53
occurring stilbenoid in fruits such as blueberries and grapes.1 Both pterostilbene and 
54
resveratrol exhibit many potential health-promoting activities,2, 
3 including 
55
anti-inflammatory,4 antioxidant,5 anti-aging,6 anti-cancer,7, 
8 anti-cardiovascular 
56
disease,9 anti-diabetic,5 and neuroprotective activities.10 Some biological activities of 
57
pterostilbene are even higher than those of resveratrol. For example, an animal study 
58
demonstrated that pterostilbene had higher ability to rejuvenate brain cells and 
59
preserve cognitive function than did resveratrol.10 In a previous study,11 pterostilbene 
60
exhibited stronger in vitro anti-inflammatory activity than resveratrol. The existence 
61
of two methoxy groups in its structure makes pterostilbene less susceptible to phase II 
62
metabolism, thus it achieves a more extensive distribution in the body. Hence 
63
pterostilbene has better metabolic stability than resveratrol. Plasma levels of 
64
pterostilbene and its metabolites were significantly higher than those of resveratrol 
65
after oral dosing. In this research, the oral bioavailability of pterostilbene was 80%, 
66
higher than that of resveratrol (20%).12 All of these factors make pterostilbene a more 
67
promising bioactive compound than resveratrol.
68
Although pterostilbene has the above mentioned advantages, its application has 
69
been limited by low aqueous solubility (approximately 20 μg/mL).13 As a 
70
consequence, it is essential to formulate a delivery system for pterostilbene before 
71
adding it into food stuff.14 Recently, many researches have reported the utilization of 
72
nanoemulsion-based delivery systems to enhance water-solubility, stability, and 
73
bioaccessibility of hydrophobic bioactive compounds. Nanoemulsion-based delivery 
74
systems have many advantages as carriers of lipophilic compounds.15-19 Generally

speaking, nanoemulsions are colloidal particulate systems with small particle size, 
76
contributing to the compound’s potential for high stability, better appearance, and 
77
better food matrix compatibility.20 In addition, small droplets have large surface areas, 
78
increasing rates of digestion in the gastrointestinal tract. Then, the digestive micelles 
79
were formed to encapsulate lipophilic bioactive compounds, potentially enhancing 
80
compounds permeability and absorption through the epithelial cells lining the small 
81
intestine. 
82
The type of carrier lipid has been reported to have a major influence on the 
83
digestibility of nanoemulsions, the efficiency of micelle formation, the 
84
bioaccessibility, and bioavailability of lipophilic compounds.21-24 For example, 
85
nanoemulsions composed of lipids rich in medium chain fatty acids may promote 
86
faster in vitro lipid digestion than long or short chain fatty acids.25 Moreover, 
87
nanoemulsions made with non-digestible oils such as orange oil, had significantly 
88
lower bioaccessibility than those prepared with digestible oils such as maize oil.21 To 
89
date, a limited number of studies have reported the use of nanoemulsion systems to 
90
deliver pterostilbene. For instance, Sun et al studied the influence of olive oil and 
91
flaxseed oil nanoemulsions on pterostilbene bioavailability using a Caco-2 cell 
92
model.23 This study showed that olive oil nanoemulsions enhanced trans-enterocyte 
93
transport of pterostilbene more efficiently than flaxseed oil nanoemulsions. 
94
This work was carried out to estimate the effect of carrier lipid composition on 
95
the physical stability, lipid digestibility, pterostilbene bioaccessibility, and 
96
pterostilbene permeability across small intestinal epithelium cells. We first 
97
determined the saturation concentrations of pterostilbene in three different lipids 
98
(medium chain triglycerides (MCT), sunflower oil, and olive oil), which vary in their 
99
chain length and unsaturation levels of fatty acids. Pterostilbene dissolved in lipid

101
Nanoemulsion delivery systems was prepared by mixing lipid phase with aqueous 
102
phase using high-pressure homogenization. These delivery systems were subjected to 
103
in vitro digestion using a gastrointestinal model simulating stomach and small 
104
intestine. The physical stability of each nanoemulsion after exposure to typical 
105
environmental stresses (pH, ionic strength, and temperature) was also tested. Finally, 
106

107
digestion of each nanoemulsion were determined using a Caco-2 cell monolayer 
108
model. To our knowledge, the current research is the first to investigate the solubility 
109
of pterostilbene in different lipid carriers, and the first to report the impact of chain 
110
length of fatty acids on pterostilbene bioaccessibility and Caco-2 cell permeability of 
111
pterostilbene in nanoemulsion-based delivery systems. This research provides 
112
important insights for developing pterostilbene-loaded nanoemulsion-based delivery 
113
systems for use in functional foods and nutraceutical supplements.

2.4. Nanoemulsions preparation
155
Nanoemulsions were prepared by a previously described high-pressure 
156
homogenization method.28 The aqueous phase of each nanoemulsion was prepared by 
157
dispersing 1% (w/w) sodium caseinate in phosphate buffer solution (pH 7.0, 10 mM). 
158
Oil phases were obtained by dissolving pterostilbene (1%, w/w) into MCT, olive oil, 
159
and sunflower oil, respectively. Coarse emulsions were prepared by mixing an 
160
aqueous phase (90%, w/w) with an oil phase (10%, w/w) using a high-speed blender 
161
(T25 digital ULTRA-TURRAX, IKA, Germany) at 12000 rpm for 3 min. Emulsions 
162
were then further homogenized using a high-pressure homogenizer (AH-BASIC, ATS 
163
Engineering Inc, Canada) three times at 500 bar. 
164

165
The mean particle size and ζ-potential of each nanoemulsion was determined as 
166
described previously29 using a Zetasizer (Nano-ZS, Malvern Instruments, UK). 
167
Samples were diluted with phosphate buffer solution (10 mM, pH 2.0-9.0) prior to 
168

182

183

184

185

186

187

188

189

190

191

194

195

196

197

3. Results and Discussion
275
3.1. Saturation concentration of pterostilbene in different lipids
276
The ability of lipid to solubilize hydrophobic bioactive compounds varies with 
277
fatty acid composition. We first determined the fatty acid composition of three lipids: 
278
MCT, olive oil, and sunflower oil. As shown in Table 1, MCT was mainly composed 
279
of medium chain length fatty acids including C8:0 (caprylic acid, 55.41%) and C10:0 
280
(capric acid, 43.84%). Olive oil and sunflower oil were mainly composed of long 
281
chain fatty acids including C18:1 (oleic acid, 70.96% and 27.22% for olive oil and 
282
sunflower oil, respectively) and C18:2 (linoleic acid, 9.78% and 61.98% for olive oil 
283
and sunflower oil, respectively). 
284
The saturation concentrations of pterostilbene in each lipid was then determined. 
285
As shown in Fig. 2, the maximum lipid solubility of pterostilbene decreased as fatty 
286
acid chain length increased: MCT (242.4 ± 10.1, mg/g) > sunflower oil (100.4 ± 3.2, 
287
mg/g) and olive oil (98.5 ± 3.7, mg/g). This phenomenon could be attributed to the 
288
“like dissolves like” principle.37 The hydroxyl group of pterostilbene is a polar group, 
289
which will have higher solubility in lipids with greater polarity. Carrier lipids with 
290
more polar groups will instigate more dipole-dipole interactions between polar groups 
291
on lipids and those on pterostilbene molecules. In this case, MCT has more polar 
292
groups per unit mass, giving it the highest capacity to solubilize pterostilbene. 
293
Sunflower oil and olive oil are similar in fatty acid chain lengths. Their main 
294
difference lies in C18:1 and C18:2 contents. Hence, the solubility of pterostilbene in 
295
sunflower oil was not significantly different (p > 0.05) than in olive oil. In our 
296
research, pterostilbene had relatively low water-solubility (7.8 ± 1.9 μg/mL), in close

480
In summary, the influence of carrier lipid composition on the physical stability, in 
481
vitro digestion, bioaccessibility, and Caco-2 cell monolayer permeability of 
482

483
saturation solubility of pterostilbene decreased as fatty acid chain length increased:

491
